content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper proposes to extend the idea of variance reduction to stabilize the sparse training.
The effectiveness of such a strategy is justified on various datasets/neural architectures/pruning methods.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
## Strength
* The paper is well-structured and well-written.
* Though the idea of extending variance reduction methods to sparse training is straightforward and has limited novelty, it is interesting to see that a simple rescaling trick works well in practice.
* The manuscript considers extensive numerical evaluations on various datasets/neural architectures/pruning methods.

## Weaknesses
1. Indeed the reviewer is concerned about the novelty and significance of the current draft, due to the simplicity of such an extension. A similar idea indeed can be found in [1], where they consider a momentum-based variance reduction method and their theoretical framework can somehow cover the case considered in the current draft.
2. It is unclear to the reviewer if the proposed tricks can be extended to other variance reduction methods or not, e.g., MVR [2], SARAH [...], SPIDER [3], and many others. If not, then the manuscript is required to compare with these variance reduction methods.

## Questions:
* Why it is necessary to include $N$ and $\alpha$ e.g. in the expression of $\eta$? Section A.5.1 is not clear enough.

## Reference
1. Optimization with Access to Auxiliary Information. https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.00395.
2. Momentum-based variance reduction in non-convex sgd. https://arxiv.org/abs/1905.10018.
3. Near-optimal non-convex optimization via stochastic path-integrated differential estimator. NeurIPS 2018.

content.title: Response to reviewer TmTX (Q1-Q2)
content.comment:
Thank you for your valuable review. Please see our responses below to clarify the main concerns.

**Q1: Indeed the reviewer is concerned about the novelty and significance of the current draft, due to the simplicity of such an extension.**

A1: The simplicity of our approach is actually one of our strengths, which can lead to the following benefits.
- Easy to implement and can be applied to most existing sparse training methods.
- Does not add much extra cost compared to SVRG.

For the novelty and significance of our work:
- Although widely used in various tasks, the time inefficiency of sparse training remains unresolved. This work provides an analysis of the causes of the slowdown and paves the way for achieving space-time co-efficiency. 

- In the paper, we shed light on the problems of increasing gradient variance and training instability in existing sparse training methods and propose a simple yet effective algorithm that greatly accelerates and stabilizes sparse training in both standard and adversarial settings, while still maintaining high final accuracy. 
- We provide both theoretical support and extensive experimental results on different datasets, architectures, and sparse training methods to demonstrate the effectiveness of our method. 

**Q2: A similar idea indeed can be found in [R1], where they consider a momentum-based variance reduction method, and their theoretical framework can somehow cover the case considered in the current draft.**

A2: Our adaptive gradient correction method is different from the momentum-based variance reduction method. We have added [R1] in the references.

(i) The momentum-based approach works well in general, but it still suffers from optimization difficulties due to sparsity constraints. 
- For example, in our baseline SGD, following the original code base, we have also added momentum to the optimizer. However, as shown in the pink curves in Figure 2, it still has training instability and convergence problems. 
- The reason is that they do not take into account the sparse and adversarial training characteristics and cannot provide an adaptive balance between old and new information. 

(ii) Our method AGENT is designed for sparse and adversarial training and can establish a finer control over how much information we should get from the old to help the new. 
- To demonstrate the importance of this fine-grained adaptive balance, we do ablation studies in Section 6.4. In "Fixed $c_t$", we set $c_t=0.1$ and test the convergence rate without the adaptive control. 
- We find that the adaptive balance (ours) outperforms "Fixed $c_t$" in almost all cases, especially in adversarial training. For standard training, "Fix $c_t$" provides similar convergence rates to our method, while ours tends to have better final scores.

[R1] Chayti, El Mahdi, and Sai Praneeth Karimireddy. "Optimization with access to auxiliary information." arXiv preprint arXiv:2206.00395 (2022).

replying_to: Replying to Response to reviewer TmTX (Q1-Q2)

content.title: Response to reviewer TmTX (Q3-Q4)
content.comment:
**Q3: It is unclear to the reviewer if the proposed tricks can be extended to other variance reduction methods or not, e.g., MVR [R2], SARAH [R3], SPIDER [R4], and many others. If not, then the manuscript is required to compare with these variance reduction methods.**

A3: We can extend our method to the suggested variance reduction methods and obtain adaptive gradient correction methods. 
- For [R2], when the variance-reduced gradient is calculated by $d_{t+1} = \nabla f(x_{t+1}, \xi_{t+1}) - (1-a_{t+1})(d_t - \nabla f(x_{t}, \xi_{t+1}))$ in their algorithm 1, we can add an adaptive weight $c_t$ on $(1-a_{t+1})(d_t - \nabla f(x_{t}, \xi_{t+1}))$. 
- For [R3], in their recursive framework $v_t = \nabla f_{i_t}(w_t) - \nabla f_{i_t}(w_{t-1}) + v_{t-1}$ in algorithm 1, we can add an adaptive weight $c_t$ on $v_{t-1} - \nabla f_{i_t}(w_{t-1})$. 
- For [R4], in their gradient calculation $v_k = \nabla f_{S_2} (x^k) - \nabla f_{S_2} (x^{k-1}) + v_{k-1}$ in algorithm 1, we can add an adaptive weight $c_t$ on $v_{k-1}- \nabla f_{S_2} (x^{k-1})$.

We have added these methods in references, thus allowing a more comprehensive discussion of related work. 

To avoid confusion, we emphasize that our work aims at accelerating sparse training rather than designing a novel variance reduction method. Therefore, the current baseline comparison between AGENT, SGD, and SVRG can demonstrate the effectiveness of our method.
- A widely-used optimizer in sparse training is SGD, which shows good performance in many tasks but has problems of slow convergence and unstable training. 
- Sparse training has its own particular difficulties in optimization, and these general variance reduction methods will be limited and cannot show all their power due to sparsity limitations. 
- We analyze the possible reasons for the time inefficiency and the challenges when applying general variance reduction methods. We find that sparse training is more sensitive to how much information we should extract from the old gradient, and it is crucial to maintain a balance between the old and new gradients. 
- We propose an adaptive gradient correction method, AGENT, to adaptively determine how much knowledge we need to learn from the old gradients to obtain more accurate gradients in sparse training.

[R2] Cutkosky, Ashok, and Francesco Orabona. "Momentum-based variance reduction in non-convex sgd." NeurIPS 2019.

[R3] Nguyen, Lam M., et al. "SARAH: A novel method for machine learning problems using stochastic recursive gradient." ICML, 2017.

[R4] Near-optimal non-convex optimization via stochastic path-integrated differential estimator. NeurIPS 2018.

**Q4: Why it is necessary to include $N$ and $\alpha$ e.g. in the expression of $\eta$? Section A.5.1 is not clear enough.**

A4:  (i) The use of $N$ and $\alpha$ is following previous work [R5], and the goal is to enable us to bound $b_{0}$ such that $b_{0} \leq \frac{2 \mu n c_{s}^2 L (e^{\frac{1}{4c_s^2 + 1}} - 1)}{N^{\frac{\alpha}{2}} (4 c_{s}^2 + 1)}$. Then, we can find a uniform bound for $\phi \geq \frac{n \nu}{L N^{\alpha}}$ after finding the bound for $b_{0}$, which is important in the following proof. 

(ii) Apart from that, the introduction of $N^{\alpha}$ in the proof can achieve the trade-off between the first and second term of our bound $E [|| g(\theta_{\pi})||^2] \leq \frac{(G(\theta_0)- G(\theta_{*})) L N^\alpha}{T n \nu } + \frac{2 \kappa \mu^2 \sigma^2}{ N^\alpha \nu m}$. If $L$ is large compared to $\sigma$, we can let $N^{\alpha}$ be relatively small to obtain a smaller bound for our method.
    
(iii) From an intuitive perspective, we can see that $N^{\alpha}$ is in the denominator of the stepsize $\eta$. When the data size $N$ is large, each mini-batch data will be a limited representation of the whole dataset. Thus, it's better to have a small stepsize $\eta$.

We have updated it in the new manuscript version to make it clearer.

[R5] Reddi, Sashank J., et al. "Stochastic variance reduction for nonconvex optimization." ICML, 2016.

content.comment:
In general, the responses have addressed most of the concerns, and the reviewer would increase the score to 6.

Some remaining questions:
1. The idea of R1 lies in leveraging an auxiliary function to approximate the expensive target function, where the approximation bias can be corrected via the momentum-based method or MVR-based method. As stated, this framework could also cover the case of a compressed model. 
    * However, it is unclear to the reviewer why the following sentence, i.e., "For example, in our baseline SGD, following the original code base, we have also added momentum to the optimizer. However, as shown in the pink curves in Figure 2, it still has training instability and convergence problems.", could be used to support the claim of "The momentum-based approach works well in general, but it still suffers from optimization difficulties due to sparsity constraints.".
2. It is encouraging if the authors can justify the generality of the proposed methods, through some empirical results, on MVR, SARAH, and SPIDER; otherwise, the significance of the contribution is a bit limited.
3. The statement "From an intuitive perspective, we can see that $N$ is in the denominator of the stepsize $\eta$. When the data size $N$ is large, each mini-batch data will be a limited representation of the whole dataset. Thus, it's better to have a small stepsize $\eta$." cannot fully convince me. For example, ImageNet is much larger than CIFAR, but the optimal stepsizes are somehow very similar.

content.title: Response to reviewer TmTX (Additional review)
content.comment:
Thank you so much for the response and valuable comments! Please see our responses below to clarify the remaining concerns.

**Q1: The idea of R1 lies in leveraging an auxiliary function to approximate the expensive target function, where the approximation bias can be corrected via the momentum-based method or MVR-based method. As stated, this framework could also cover the case of a compressed model.**
- **However, it is unclear to the reviewer why the following sentence, i.e., "For example, in our baseline SGD, following the original code base, we have also added momentum to the optimizer. However, as shown in the pink curves in Figure 2, it still has training instability and convergence problems.", could be used to support the claim of "The momentum-based approach works well in general, but it still suffers from optimization difficulties due to sparsity constraints.".**

A1: Momentum-based methods either do not provide adaptive gradients or do not provide adaptivity in terms of gradient correlation. Therefore, they may not provide the appropriate $c_t$ in sparse training.

(i) SGD with momentum [R1] cannot provide adaptive gradients to control the balance between new and old gradients more finely.
- The gradient update is formulated as $d_t = (1-a) d_{t-1} + a \nabla f(x_t, \xi_t)$. 
- The weight between the new and old gradients is a constant, and how much information we get from the old gradients does not change. 

(ii) MVR-based method [R1] can give adaptive gradients, but it cannot adjust the weights between the new and old gradients to accommodate the challenges of sparse training.
- The gradient update is given by $d_t = (1-a_t) d_{t-1} + a_t \nabla f(x_t, \xi_t) + (1-a_t)(\nabla f(x_t, \xi_t) - \nabla f(x_{t-1}, \xi_t))$, where $a_t=\frac{k}{(w + \sum_{i=1}^t G_t^2)^{1/3}}$ and $G_t = \vert\vert\nabla f(x_t, \xi_t)\vert\vert$. 
- The weights between the new and the old gradient depend on the magnitude of the new gradient $G_t$. When $G_t$ is large, the algorithm will put more weight on the old gradient. If $G_t$ is small, the algorithm will put more weight on the new gradient.
- Adaptation based on the gradient magnitude does not control how much we should add to the old gradients in terms of their correlation. However, as shown in Equation (3) in the manuscript, $c_t^*$ is related to the correlation and we cannot estimate it properly by MVR in sparse training.

[R1] Cutkosky, Ashok, and Francesco Orabona. "Momentum-based variance reduction in non-convex sgd." NeurIPS (2019).


**Q2: It is encouraging if the authors can justify the generality of the proposed methods, through some empirical results, on MVR, SARAH, and SPIDER; otherwise, the significance of the contribution is a bit limited.**

We add experiments with MVR [R1] on 99% sparse VGG-C (SET-ITOP). As shown in the table below, our AGENT + MVR has a faster convergence rate compared to MVR.
| Epoch |  20 |  40 |  70 |  90 |  140 |  200  |
| :---------: | -----: | -----: | -----: | -----: | -----: | -----: |
| MVR (VGG-C, SET-ITOP)| 62.6| 66.8| 69.8| 71.2| 73.5| 74.4 |
| AGENT+MVR (VGG-C, SET-ITOP) | **71.6** | **75.7** | **77.9** | **79.1** | **82.3** | **82.3** |

We will add experiments about SARAH and SPIDER in our final version.

[R1] Cutkosky, Ashok, and Francesco Orabona. "Momentum-based variance reduction in non-convex sgd." NeurIPS (2019).


**Q3: The statement "From an intuitive perspective, we can see that is in the denominator of the stepsize. When the data size is large, each mini-batch data will be a limited representation of the whole dataset. Thus, it's better to have a small stepsize ." cannot fully convince me. For example, ImageNet is much larger than CIFAR, but the optimal stepsizes are somehow very similar.**

(i) Yes, we agree that the optimal step sizes for large and small data sets are very similar to some extent. The reason is that there are other factors that affect $\eta=\frac{\mu n }{L N^{\alpha}}$, such as $\mu$ and $L$. Therefore, larger $N$ may not lead to smaler $\eta$.

(ii) The limited representativeness of the entire data set in a small batch can also be reflected in two other aspects.
- As shown by the bound in Theorem 1, a larger $N$ makes $E [|| g(\theta_{\pi})||^2]$ larger.
$$
 E [|| g(\theta_{\pi})||^2] \leq \frac{(G(\theta_0)- G(\theta_{*})) L N^\alpha}{T n \nu } + \frac{2 \kappa \mu^2 \sigma^2}{ N^\alpha m \nu }.
$$
- From an intuitive point of view, we need more iterations to train ImageNet data than CIFAR-10 or CIFAR-100 data, which indicates that each small batch has a smaller proportion of information.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors propose a modified version of the adaptive gradient method SVRG, denoted AGENT, for sparse neural networks motivated by the claim that with sparse neural networks gradients across iterations have lower correlation/higher variance than in dense neural networks. The authors add two hyperparameters to SVRG, the main parameter $c_t$ is tuned to effectively discount (or not) the old gradient information used in SVRG. This hyperparameter is updated in a momentum-like manner at the end of each training epoch based on an approximation of the correct ($c^*_t$) for that iteration approximated using a subset of training samples and the covariance of the loss on the new and old gradients. An additional parameter, $\gamma$ is used to further downweight $c_t$ in practice to avoid biased gradients and error from poor approximation of $c^*_t$. The authors apply their optimization method to several dynamic sparse training methods, including BSR-Net, RigL and ITOP, and evaluate the performance of their optimizer with these DST training methods on CIFAR-10/100, SVHN and ImageNet over a variety of models including ResNets, WideResNets and VGG.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
# Strengths
* Strong experimental results, with decreased convergence time demonstrated with the proposed method, while maintaining or for high-sparsity increasing generalization compared to SGD/vanilla SVRG.
* Experiments are performed by using the AGENT optimizer with BSR-Net, RigL and ITOP, the latter two at least are relevant and good baselines.
* Experiments performed on a range of suitable models including ResNet-18, ResNet-50 and WideResNet-28-4 (except VGG which really has no place in sparsity papers in 2022 given how over-parameterized it is).
* Experiments performed on a range of suitable datasets, including CIFAR-10/100, SVHN and ImageNet.

# Weaknesses
* No analysis or comparison with other similar adaptive gradient methods, e.g. Adam, which is used in the RigL paper for language tasks as-is, and doesn't seem to present any issues. The authors to compare with vanilla SVRG, but it's conceivable there is an issue with SVRG in dynamic sparse neural networks not present in alternative (and frankly simpler/cheaper) adaptive gradient methods. 
* The motivation of this work is that gradients across iterations/mini-batches have less correlation in sparse training methods in general  than in dense models. This is a surprising & interesting claim to make, as we would expect serious training issues when performing SGD with weakly correlated gradients over iterations, and yet there are many sparse training methods that seem to converge fine with SGD (albeit yes slower). I could believe the correlation is reduced slightly compared to dense, slowing down convergence, but we aren't given any quantification of this supposed problem to judge, and I really searched through the work as I'm genuinely interested in this claim. The single citation associated with the claim sparsity leads to "larger variance" (of I assume gradients) is (Hoefler et al), which is a survey paper, and I can't identify which of the 300 works within that the authors might be actually considering. Note to authors: you should cite papers found within the survey rather than survey papers alone for this reason.
* The authors do have further reasoning behind this weakly correlated gradients statement as presented in the appendix B6. Here the author's argument is that across mask changes we would expect weaker correlation between disparate weights. However, many sparse training methods do not change the mask, or change it rarely, so the claim appears to only have validity potentially for DST methods (which are indeed what the authors focus on in their results). Even DST methods only change the mask at mask update steps, e.g. in RigL every 100 iterations until 75% of training is done, and then not changed for the remainder of training - i.e. the mask only changes a total of 240 times over training, and not at all for the last quarter. It would be reasonable to assume this problem only occurs for a short period after the mask update step in these models. Why not show an analysis of the correlation of gradients while training around a mask update to better understand this problem. Why not then only not change $c^t$ for iterations occurring for a short time after the mask update rather than every epoch?
* Although the authors claim in the main paper there is empirical evidence for this weak correlation, the empirical analysis in appendix B6 appears to be very limited and, as written, I have trouble understanding any details of. It seems the authors used checkpoints from RigL and a dense model (how is the dense model related to RigL?), and measured the correlation of the "gradients of the original weights and new weights" while adding noise to the weights. What specifically are the original weights and new weights in this context (i.e. just sampled from an arbitrary epoch during training?), and why would we want to add noise?
* $\gamma$ is effectively just multiplier on $c_t$ (and hence the old gradients) in the optimizer step, in other words with the default of $\gamma=0.1$, the effective range of this weighting of the old gradient, or $c_t$ is actually *0--0.1*. This throws a lot of the motivation of AGENT into question as effectively it is restricted to using 10% of the old gradient information maximum, and it seems very unlikely between steps are *that* weakly correlated. If the aim as stated was to avoid introducing large variance/bias due to error in approximating $c_t$, wouldn't reducing the learning rate (i.e. also scaling both the the new and old gradient information) make more sense?
* Equation (1) presents the SVRG update rule, but if $g_i(\mathbf{\theta_t}) \approx g_i(\mathbf{\tilde{\theta}})$, then this is essentially subtracting two very similar numbers, and if gradients are large this results in a loss of precision in floating point arithmetic (i.e. cancellation). Having $\gamma$ = 0.1 ensures this never occours, so I wonder if the utility of $\gamma$ has more to do with numerical stability myself...
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Aside from the issues I have in understanding parts of the paper as presented in Strengths and Weaknesses, most of the paper was relatively well-written, and likely AGENT itself is reproducible as it's a relatively simple modification of AVRG

There are however some inconsistencies in the math and the equation formatting that need to be corrected, for example, in equations (1) and (2), $g_i$ alternates between being a vector (bolded) and not. In explaining Equation (1) $\tilde{g}$ is described as the "full gradients", and then defined below in math as being the loss $\tilde{g} = G(\tilde{\theta})$.
content.summary_of_the_review: While the empirical results of this work appear to be interesting, and perhaps even significant, the method itself is not motivated or explained in a way that is anywhere near convincing. In particular the main motivation of the method (that sparse training gradients are less correlated than dense) has little evidence, and the only reasoning given would only apply to dynamic sparse training methods such as RigL, and even then only on mask update steps (while the paper claims this for all sparse training). Even giving the authors the benefit of bout, while weighting/down-weighting the old gradients in the SVRG method would make sense if the motivation were true, the authors always significantly down-weight the old gradient information (only) massively given the $\gamma$ hyperparameter, and this is not well-justified.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.title: Response to reviewer UoMt (Q1-Q2)
content.comment:
Thank you for the review and for bringing up these questions. Please see our responses below to clarify the main concerns.

**Q1: No analysis or comparison with other similar adaptive gradient methods, e.g. Adam. The authors compare it with vanilla SVRG, but it's conceivable there is an issue with SVRG in dynamic sparse neural networks not present in alternative (and frankly simpler/cheaper) adaptive gradient methods.**

A1: (i) The faster convergence rate brought by our AGENT compared to SGD and SVRG can support our AGENT's success in accelerating sparse training. Existing work on variance reduction is mainly compared to SGD and baseline methods like SVRG and SAGA [R1, R2, R3, R4].

(ii) In addition, we add experiments to compare our AGENT with Adam and find that our method still has a faster convergence rate compared to Adam (shown in Appendix B.9). 

(iii) We also summarize the test accuracy after training 20, 40, 70, 90, 140, and 200 epochs on CIFAR-10 using either our AGENT or Adam at 99% sparsity. As shown in the table below, AGENT has almost higher accuracy than Adam for the same number of epochs, indicating a faster convergence rate.

| Epoch |  20 |  40 |  70 |  90 |  140 |  200  |
| :---------: | -----: | -----: | -----: | -----: | -----: | -----: |
| Adam (VGG-C, SET-ITOP)| 73.0| 76.4| 76.9| 77.8| 86.1| 86.8 |
| AGENT (VGG-C, SET-ITOP) | **75.9**| **79.3**| **82.5**| **81.7**| **87.5**| **88.4** |
| Adam (ResNet-34, SET-ITOP)| 50.3| 41.7| 57.3| 47.4| 77.3| 84.8 |
| AGENT (ResNet-34, SET-ITOP) | **83.0**| **85.9**| **84.9**| **87.5**| **92.3**| **92.7** |
| Adam (VGG-C, RigL-ITOP)| **72.9**| 72.2| **77.0**| 60.8| 86.7| 88.1 |
| AGENT (VGG-C, RigL-ITOP) | 67.9| **76.2**| 75.2| **74.5**| **87.2**| **88.7** |
| Adam (ResNet-34, RigL-ITOP)| 50.8| 56.6| 52.9| 39.1| 77.5| 83.4 |
| AGENT (ResNet-34, RigL-ITOP) | **81.3**| **85.5**| **82.6**| **80.3**| **91.9**| **92.9** |

The main reason is that our AGENT is designed for sparse training and is tailored to the characteristics of sparse training. 
- Challenge in sparse training: When old information is used to correct the gradients, the main problem is the reduced correlation between the old and new gradients. 
- Our AGENT approximates the correlation and adds an adaptive weight to the old gradient to establish a balance between the old and new gradients. 
- Previous adaptive gradient methods, such as Adam, are not designed for sparse training. Although they also provide adaptive gradients, their adaptivity is different and does not take correlation into account.

[R1] Zou, D., Xu, P., & Gu, Q. (2018). Subsampled stochastic variance-reduced gradient Langevin dynamics. UAI.

[R2] Defazio, A., Bach, F., & Lacoste-Julien, S. (2014). SAGA: A fast incremental gradient method with support for non-strongly convex composite objectives. NeurIPS.

[R3] Allen-Zhu, Z., & Hazan, E. (2016). Variance Reduction for Faster Non-Convex Optimization. ICML.

[R4] Elibol, M., Lei, L., & Jordan, M. I. (2020). Variance Reduction With Sparse Gradients. ICLR.

**Q2: The motivation of this work is that gradients across iterations/mini-batches have less correlation in sparse training methods in general than in dense models.  I could believe the correlation is reduced slightly compared to dense, slowing down convergence, but we aren't given any quantification of this supposed problem to judge. The single citation associated with the claim sparsity leads to "larger variance" (of I assume gradients) is (Hoefler et al), which is a survey paper.**

A2: (i) To support our claim of weaker correlations in sparse training, we include a discussion and experimental results in Appendix B.6, which will be discussed in A3 and A4.

(ii) To support our claim of "larger variance", we cite three related references [R5, R6, R7] in the third paragraph of the introduction.
- [R5] is a survey paper, we refer to Section 5.3.2, where it mentions that "sparsification can increase the variance in the resulting sparse gradients and hence slow convergence". 
- [R6] studied the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of sparse models and showed sparser models have smaller SNR, indicating the presence of large variance and noise in the sparse training.
- [R7] also pointed out the increase in variance due to quantization, which, although not directly related to sparse training, is highlighting the potential variance increase problem when compressing the model.

[R5] Hoefler, Torsten, et al. "Sparsity in Deep Learning: Pruning and growth for efficient inference and training in neural networks." J. Mach. Learn. Res. 22.241 (2021): 1-124.

[R6] Graesser, L., Evci, U., Elsen, E., & Castro, P. S. (2022). The State of Sparse Training in Deep Reinforcement Learning. ICML.

[R7]Alistarh, Dan, et al. "QSGD: Communication-efficient SGD via gradient quantization and encoding." NeurIPS (2017).

content.title: Response to reviewer UoMt (Q3-Q4)
content.comment:
**Q3: The authors do have further reasoning behind this weakly correlated gradients statement as presented in appendix B6. Here the author's argument is that across mask changes we would expect a weaker correlation between disparate weights. Why not show an analysis of the correlation of gradients when the mask does not change?**

A3: The correlation of the gradients becomes weaker regardless of whether the mask is changed or not (discussion is included in Appendix B.6).

(i) When the mask is not changed: 
- As we know, $c_t^* = \frac{\text{Cov}(g_{\text{new}}, g_{\text{old}})}{\text{Var}(g_{\text{old}})}$. Even if $\text{Cov}(g_{\text{new}}, g_{\text{old}})$ does not decrease, the variance $\text{Var}(g_{\text{old}})$ increases in sparse training, leading to a decrease in $c_t^*$. 
- Additional experiments in Appendix B.6 also demonstrate a weaker correlation when the mask is not changed.

(i) When the mask is changed: In our previous discussion, there are three cases of sparse training.
- First, if current weights are pruned, we do not need to consider their correlation because we do not need to update the current weights using the corresponding previous weights. 

- Second, if current weights are not pruned but previous weights are pruned, the previous weights are zero and the difference between the two weights is relatively large, leading to a lower relevance. 
- Third, if neither the current nor the previous weights are pruned, which weights are pruned can still change significantly, leading to large changes in the current and previous models. Thus, the correlation between the current and previous gradients of the weights we are considering will be relatively small.

**Q4: Although the authors claim in the main paper there is empirical evidence for this weak correlation, the empirical analysis in appendix B6 appears to be very limited and, as written, I have trouble understanding any details.**

A4: In Appendix B.6, we empirically demonstrate the weaker correlation in sparse training when the mask is not changed.

(i) Experiment description:
- We begin with fully-trained checkpoints from ResNet-50 on CIFAR-100 with RigL and SET at 0%, 50%, 80%, 90%, and 95% sparsity.
- We calculate and store the gradient of each weight on all training data.
- We add Gaussian perturbations (std = 0.015) to all the weights and calculate the gradients again.
- We calculate the correlation between the gradient of the new perturbed weights and the old original weights.

(ii) Experiment illustration:
- As we know, there is always a difference between the old and new weights. 
- If the gradients become very different after adding some small noise to the weights, the new and old gradients will tend to have smaller correlations. If the gradients do not change a lot after adding some small noise, the old and new gradients will have a higher correlation.
- Thus, we add Gaussian noise to the weights to simulate the difference between the new and old gradients.

(iii) Experiment results: As shown in the table below, the correlation decreases with increasing sparsity, which indicates a weaker correlation in sparse training and supports our claim.

| Sparsity |  0%  |  50%  |  80%  |  90%  |  95%  | 
| --------- | ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- | 
| ResNet-50, CIFAR-100 (RigL) | 0.6005 | 0.4564 | 0.3217 | 0.1886 | 0.1590 |
| ResNet-50, CIFAR-100 (SET) | 0.6005 | 0.4535 | 0.2528 | 0.1763 | 0.1195 | 

We have updated it in the new manuscript version.

content.title: Response to reviewer UoMt (Q5-Q7)
content.comment:
**Q5: $\gamma=0.1$ throws a lot of the motivation of AGENT into question as effectively it is restricted to using 10\% of the old gradient information maximum, and it seems very unlikely between steps are that weakly correlated. Wouldn't reducing the learning rate (i.e. also scaling both the new and old gradient information) make more sense?**

A5: We politely disagree with the reviewer. Reducing the learning rate is not effective in accelerating sparse training, and setting $\gamma=01$ is reasonable, especially in adversarial settings.

(i) For accelerating by reducing the learning rate:
-  Since it will reduce both the signal and noise, the signal-to-noise ratio cannot be increased and the sparse training cannot be accelerated.
-  Empirically, we find that reducing the learning rate does not work (included in Appendix B.10). We compare our AGENT with "Reduce LR", where we remove the scaling parameter $\gamma$ from AGENT and set the learning rate to 0.1 times the original one.
- As shown in the table below, reducing the learning rate can lead to a comparable convergence rate in the early stage. However, it slows down the later stages of training and leads to sub-optimal final accuracy.

| Epoch |  20| 80| 130| 180| 240 |
| :---------: | -----: | -----: | -----: | -----: | -----: | 
| Reduce LR (VGG-C, SET-ITOP)| **76.5**| 81.3| 84.6| 85.5| 85.5| 
| AGENT (VGG-C, SET-ITOP) | 76.1| **81.5**| **87.6**| **87.1**| **88.6**| 
| Reduce LR (ResNet-34, SET-ITOP)| 81.4| **85.9**| 89.3| 89.5| 89.8 |
| AGENT (ResNet-34, SET-ITOP) | **83.0**|  85.6|  **92.0**|  **92.3**|  **92.5**| 

(ii) For the choice of $\gamma$:
- The motivation of $\gamma$ is to avoid introducing large variance due to error in approximating $c_t$ and bias due to the adversarial training. 
- The true correlation depends on many factors such as the dataset, architecture, and sparsity. In some cases, it can be greater or smaller than 10%.
- For the value of $\gamma$, it is a hyperparameter and we can choose different values for different settings. In our case, for simplicity, we choose $\gamma=0.1$ for all the settings and find that it works well and accelerates the convergence.
- If we tune the value of $\gamma$ for different settings according to their corresponding correlations, it is possible to obtain faster convergence rates.

**Q6: Equation (1) presents the SVRG update rule, but if $g_i(\theta_t) \approx g_i(\widetilde{\theta})$, then this is essentially subtracting two very similar numbers, and if gradients are large this results in a loss of precision in floating point arithmetic (i.e. cancellation). Having  = 0.1 ensures this never occurs, so I wonder if the utility of  has more to do with numerical stability myself...**

A6: We politely disagree with the reviewer. The utility of our AGENT is independent of numerical stability.

In SVRG, the corrected gradient is expressed as $\hat{g}(\theta_t) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i \in \textbf{B}_t} (g_i(\theta_t)-  g_i(\tilde{\theta})) + \tilde{g}.$

(i) If $g_i(\theta_t) \approx g_i(\widetilde{\theta})$, there will be a high correlation between the new and old gradients, which suggests that $\widetilde{g}$ will be a good approximation to the true full gradient. Thus, although $g_i(\theta_t) - g_i(\widetilde{\theta})\approx 0$, $\hat{g}(\theta_t)$ will be closed to $\widetilde{g}$, which is closed to the true full gradient.

(ii) In addition, $g_i(\theta_t) \approx g_i(\widetilde{\theta})$ is unlikely to happen due to the weak correlation in sparse training. 

Therefore, the utility of our AGENT is independent of numerical stability.

**Q7: There are however some inconsistencies in the math and the equation formatting that need to be corrected, for example, in equations (1) and (2), $g_i$ alternates between being a vector (bolded) and not. In explaining Equation (1) $\widetilde{g}$ is described as the "full gradients", and then defined below in math as being the loss $\widetilde{g}=G(\widetilde{\theta})$.**

A7: Thanks for pointing out the typos. We have updated them in the new manuscript.

content.comment:
Q3. (i) "when the mask is not changed"... "the variance $Var(g_{old}$ increases in sparse training", again this is the same argument as in Q2, but I have yet to see evidence of this. 

(ii) "When the mask is changed".
This answer doesn't unfortunately seem to relate to my questions aside from repeating the explanation from B.6 that when the mask changes, there is a lower correlation between weights, and I do agree with this observation itself. However, as I pointed out in my original review, in reality masks don't change very often in sparse neural network training, and so this wouldn't appear to anywhere near the big problem your motivation makes it out to be. I was hoping you would clarify here why you think this is a problem outside of the few iterations close to infrequent mask updates in DST methods.

Q4. I'm very confused by the analysis done here, given the authors are trying to demonstrate the motivation (i.e. "sparse training results in lower correlation of gradients across training iterations than in dense training"). If this is the case, should it not be as simple as showing the correlation between gradients during training of a dense and sparse model with the same number of (active) weights?

Furthermore, the analysis does not compare with dense models, only two different DST methods. I'm also quite unclear as to why the specific approach of adding Gaussian noise to a pre-trained model was decided upon to demonstrate this, although maybe that would still be something to consider if compared to a dense model (with similar number of weights).

First thanks to the authors for their feedback, and apologies for the late response to this. I'll respond to each point using the question numbers used by the authors below.

Q1: I think this could present a good baseline or comparison, strengthens the results significantly. However the results are a bit curious in that there are lots of seeming outliers at epoch 90 for Adam, i.e. Adam (VGG-C, RigL-ITOP), Adam (ResNet-34, RigL-ITOP) and Adam (ResNet-34, SET-ITOP) at 90 epochs show significant drops in performance relative to the closest epochs?

Q2. To be clear I'm looking for quantitative evidence that sparsity induces less correlation across iterations. [R5] is a statement pulled from a survey paper apparently without anything to back it up, [R7] is a stretch, quantization is quite unrelated as you identify. [R6] is closest to being relevant to this motivation/claim, but it's in a very different context of Reinforcement Learning which is unlike anything this paper looks at empirically. In any case you should revise the citation of [R6] to make the connection clear, and remove or at least clarify the other references as they don't seem to be relevant or support the associated claim.

Unfortunately I did not find this rebuttal point very convincing, as you still have yet to point out clear quantitative results from previous work showing that SGD + Deep Learning for a benchmark classification task shows high variance gradients in sparse neural networks compared to dense neural networks. Given this is the primary motivation of your work, this is an issue.

content.title: Response to reviewer d7Lx (Q1-Q5)
content.comment:
Thank you for the valuable comments and for acknowledging the value of our work. Please find our responses to the questions as follows.

**Q1: $\text{Var}$ and $\text{Cov}$ in Equations (3) and (4) are not clearly defined, especially what random variable is taken expectation on.**

A1: The $\text{Var}$ and $\text{Cov}$ denotes variance and covariance, which are taking expectation w.r.t. the random subset $B$.

**Q2: In Equation (4), $G(B|\theta)$ is also undefined. I could only find the definition of $G(x|\theta)$, which uses ; instead of | and takes a single sample $\textbf{X}$ instead of a subset of samples $\textbf{B}$ as input.**

A2: We have unified the notations, using "$|$" instead of "$;$" in the loss function $G$. Thus, 
$G(B|\theta)=(\sum_{x\in B}G(\textbf{x}|\theta_t))/|B|$ is the average loss on the mini-batch data $B$ given parameter $\theta_t$, where $|B|$ is the batch size and $G(\textbf{x}|\theta_t)$ is the loss on single sample $\textbf{x}$. 

**Q3: Furthermore, it is unclear how the subset $B$ is sampled, because in Algorithm 1, sampling the mini-batch data $B_t$ happens after $\hat{c}_t^{*}$ is calculated. If $B$ is a random subset, does it mean that $\text{Var}$ and $\text{Cov}$ are taking expectation w.r.t. $B$?**

A3: (i) The mini-batch data $B$ can be viewed as a random subset that is uniformly sampled from the full dataset. 

(ii) Yes, $\text{Var}$ and $\text{Cov}$ are taking expectation w.r.t. the random subset $B$.

(iii) Calculating $\widehat{c}_t^*$ in each iteration is too expensive. Thus, we calculate it at the beginning of each epoch before sampling the mini-batch data and use it as an approximation for the following epoch.

**Q4: If so, doesn't that mean that we have to go through the entire dataset to calculate $\text{Var}$ and $\text{Cov}$ in Equation (4)? Or, are they just taking the average over the samples in $B$?**

A4: We have to go through the entire dataset to calculate $\text{Var}$ and $\text{Cov}$ in Equation (4), which will increase the cost a lot if we do it in each iteration. Thus, we calculate it at the beginning of each epoch and use it as an approximation for the following epoch.

**Q5: It seems that in the theoretical analysis of convergence, a constant $c$ is used. I understand using constant makes the proof much easier. However, such a mismatch weakens the significance and contribution of the theoretical analysis.**

A5: Treating $c$ as a constant is still aligned with our practical algorithm and does not weaken the significance and contribution of the theoretical analysis.

(i) In our Algorithm 1, $\widehat{c}_t^*$ is actually a fixed constant within each epoch, which can be different in different epochs. Since it is too expensive to compute the exact $\widehat{c}_t^*$ in each iteration, we compute it at the beginning of each epoch and use it as an approximation in the following epoch. 

(ii) As for our proof, we first show the convergence rate of one arbitrary training epoch. In this step, treating $c$ as a constant is aligned with our practical algorithm. 

(iii) Then, when we extend the results of one epoch to the whole epoch, we establish an upper bound for different $c$ in each epoch. Thus, the bound can be applied when $c$ differs across epochs, which enables our theoretical analysis consistent with our practical algorithm.

We agree that the constant $c$ makes the proof easier, and we will think about how to include a dynamic $c$ in future studies.

content.title: Response to reviewer vxdp (Q1-Q6)
content.comment:
Thank you for your valuable review. Please see our responses below to clarify the main concerns.

**Q1: It is not clear from the main experimental section of the paper if the results are statistically significant as the differences at the end of the training seem quite small (e.g., in Table 2).**

A1: Tables 2 and 3 are presented to show that the accuracy of our AGENT is comparable to that of the original sparse training method. Since our AGENT is designed to accelerate sparse training, our goal is to make the model converge faster with comparable accuracy, rather than achieving significantly higher final accuracy. As shown in Tables 2 and 3, the accuracy is comparable to the baseline sparse training method after using our AGENT.

**Q2: The proposed method seems to perform relatively well on smaller datasets, but not on larger ones. It is true that the performance of the proposed method is similar to the baseline and perhaps smoother. Do you have any idea why this is happening? Does it also hold for other sparsity levels?**

A2: Our method AGENT works for both small and large datasets, and the advantages may appear slightly different in different settings.

(i) Theoretically, we prove that our method provides tighter bounds than the baseline method, demonstrating its ability in training speedup. Since we do not limit the size of the dataset in our proof, it can be applied to both small and large datasets. 

(ii) Empirically, the smoother curve for the larger dataset ImageNet is a slightly different manifestation of the strengths of our AGENT. If we use SVRG in this case, we will not only fail to train stably but also slow down the training speed. In contrast, our AGENT can solve the limitation of SVRG. 

(iii) For other sparsity levels, we can expect advantages of our AGENT, in terms of acceleration or stability. Moreover, we can expect more significant speedups at different sparsity levels with more hyperparameter tuning, as the speedups are guaranteed by theoretical proof. We will include more results on larger datasets in the final version.

**Q3: Considering, among other aspects, also the above bullet point, perhaps a more comprehensive evaluation shall be done. I suggest moving outside convolutional layers and study also other types of layers (e.g., fully connected)**

A3: (i) The model architectures used in our current experiments are already comprehensive and include ResNet, Wide-ResNet, and VGG-16. They are widely used in current sparse training methods [R1, R2, R3]. 

(ii) In addition, ResNet, Wide-ResNet, and VGG-16 have both convolutional layers and fully connected layers in their architectures, which can clarify the reviewer's concern. 

Thus, current experiments can demonstrate the acceleration effect of our method in different model architectures. We will try more different types of model architectures in our future study. 

[R1] Evci, Utku, et al. "Rigging the lottery: Making all tickets winners." ICML, 2020.

[R2] Liu, Shiwei, et al. "Do we actually need dense over-parameterization? in-time over-parameterization in sparse training." ICML, 2021.

[R3] Liu, Junjie, et al. "Dynamic sparse training: Find efficient sparse network from scratch with trainable masked layers." ICLR. 2020.

**Q4: The last paragraph on page 1 refers, I believe, more to pruning (as classified in the previous paragraph), while the focus of the paper seems to be mainly on dynamic sparse training. Is my understanding correct?**

A4: We politely disagree with the reviewer. The paragraph is to discuss possible side effects when adding high sparsity to the model, including:
- Increase in gradient variance.
- Increase in training instability.
- Decrease in model robustness.

These side effects can occur in both pruning and dynamic sparse training methods. Our paper focuses on dynamic sparse training, which is within the influence of these side effects.

**Q5: “Sparse training …. is one of the most popular methods” – it is rather a class of methods in my opinion.**

A5: Yes, it is a class of methods. We have updated our statement.

**Q6: “…and previous gradient gradient based on…”; “…random selection, weight sign, and random selection…”; Figures 2d and 4d doesn’t seem alright. Or perhaps their legends?**

A6: Thank you for pointing out these typos in our manuscript and legends. We have corrected them in the new version of the manuscript.

content.title: Common Response to all Reviewers
content.comment:
We thank all reviewers for their constructive reviews. The main contributions of this work as stated by the reviewers are as follows:

- The proposed adaptive gradient correction method to accelerate sparse training is interesting and novel **[Reviewer vxdp, d7Lx]**
- The theoretical analysis is provided **[Reviewer d7Lx]**
- Extensive experiments on multiple sparse training pipelines, datasets, and model architecture are conducted and show good performance **[Reviewer vxdp, d7Lx, UoMt, TmTX]**
- The paper is clearly-written **[Reviewer vxdp, UoMt]**
- Reproducible (submitted code with running instructions) **[Reviewer vxdp, d7Lx, UoMt, TmTX]**

We would like to emphasize the significant contribution of this paper to sparse training. 

Although widely used in various tasks, the time inefficiency of sparse training remains unresolved. This work provides an analysis of the causes of the slowdown and paves the way for achieving space-time co-efficiency. In the paper, we shed light on the problems of increasing gradient variance and training instability in existing sparse training methods and propose a simple yet effective algorithm that greatly accelerates and stabilizes sparse training in both standard and adversarial settings, while still maintaining high final accuracy. We provide both theoretical support and extensive experimental results on different datasets, architectures, and sparse training methods to demonstrate the effectiveness of our method. Our method can be applied to most existing sparse training methods. We believe this work is important for efficient and stable sparse training and hope the reviewers will consider our response in their final evaluation.
